body_markdown:
An interesting conundrum in motorsports is the outright speed of a vehicle compared to the perceived level of effort the driver must exert to achieve said speed. Listen to any modern race broadcast that includes radio clips or interviews from drivers, and often you’ll hear how difficult it is to drive a car while maintaining track position. It’s easy to understand that some drivers know how to get more out of a given car than anyone else, but not all race cars are created equal. What about the “untamable” or otherwise notoriously difficult vintage race cars—or motorcycles, for that matter?


While I could only be so lucky as to explore the answer, we can refer to the first-hand experience of motorcycle racer and[YouTuber Taylor Mackenzie,](https://youtu.be/CXam6HY30Kk?si=0_qizuiDBsac3Fln) who not only had access to a race-winning vintage Grand Prix machine but also access to the team and the rider fielding it during a vintage race weekend at the Assen circuit in the Netherlands.


The bike itself is a true piece of racing history: The 1989 Suzuki RGV500 ridden by Kevin Schwantz, who went on to win the 500cc world championship in 1993. Schwantz was a magician at late braking and even at the time had a style that clearly worked on bikes that were not easy to ride fast. Packing a two-stroke, 500cc, V-4 power plant, this is a bike from the “unridable” era of motorcycle racing.


The top level of motorsport has never been easy, but can one era eclipse the rest?


Well, on paper, yes. The two-stroke, 500cc bikes of the late 1980s and 1990s GP era were lithe machines that easily tipped the scaled under 300 pounds and could pack 165 horsepower or more. The graph of their powerband resembled a ski jump, and its judicious application was controlled only by the rider’s right wrist. These are prototype machines, not production-based ones, and the materials and designs used in their construction highlight that fact. While we look at them and see materials that now don’t seem very exotic (such as the aluminum used for this bike’s frame), these machines were cutting edge at the time and yet to be fully proven or tamed. If you look at the finish rate for many of the races in this era, you’ll see that high-side crashes were far more common than they are today.


On track, the RGV looks as at home as ever.


Taylor Mackenzie


On the starting line next to some seriously fast riders and machines.


Taylor Mackenzie


The 1989 bike is easy to spot by both exhausts on the right side, as this was the first year for this swingarm design.


Taylor Mackenzie


More interesting is when these bikes appeared: It took a long time for the racing world to create beasts that were nearly beyond human control. Motorcycle racing had been going on for several decades by the 1980s, and this was the first time the machines were described as “too much.” And that descriptor appears accurate today. Don’t take my word for it; Mackenzie and fellow rider[Danny Webb](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dbl3jOpDYNr/?hl=en&img_index=1) are quick to point out that even their experience on the bike should be taken with a grain of salt due to the modern tires mounted front and back. It’s one thing to reckon with the suspension geometry of the late 1980s, the power delivery of a V-4 two-stroke, and the weight of knowing you’re riding a valuable piece of motorsport history, but even Mackenzie and Webb admit the tire technology has come so far that it alone brings the bike into the ballpark of rideability. However, just because you can safely operate a vehicle doesn’t guarantee that you can ride (or drive) it *quickly* .


Time, however, is on our side when interacting with these bikes. Since this bike was new, we’ve benefited from an additional four decades of learning and experimenting, and not only in tire development. Physics is another area; today, we better understand how motorcycles work and how rider and motorcycle interact on track. Most new riders these days can have a better grasp of track theory than some previous GP champions, since those GP champions happily teach everything they know to anyone curious enough to pay attention. That said, all the theory in the world doesn’t ensure that you can interact with the machine or keep pace with an entire grid of them.


The wild, 500cc machines of decades past were wild then and are likely still otherworldly to experience now, but for different reasons than you might expect. Though modern machines do more for the rider than ever, no one is going to call a modern GP machine simple to ride.


But I will, if doing so means that someone with the right machine wants to prove me wrong …
